meta.title: Who really said "When you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes also into you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Nietzsche — Beyond Good and Evil (1886), aphorism 146. The German is public domain, but the modern English wording tracks R. J. Hollingdale's 1973 translation, which is not. Helen Zimmern's 1906 version is the free alternative.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes also into you'?
meta.ogDescription: Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil (1886), §146 — and it opens with the monsters. The German is free to reuse; the English wording you know probably isn't.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Jenseits von Gut und Böse (Beyond Good and Evil), 1886, aphorism 146 — and it is only the second half of the thought. The first half is the one about monsters: “Wer mit Ungeheuern kämpft, mag zusehn, dass er nicht dabei zum Ungeheuer wird.” The English wording in circulation is not the public-domain translation; it tracks R. J. Hollingdale’s of 1973.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Jenseits von Gut und Böse (Beyond Good and Evil), aphorism 146

source.excerpt: Wer mit Ungeheuern kämpft, mag zusehn, dass er nicht dabei zum Ungeheuer wird. Und wenn du lange in einen Abgrund blickst, blickt der Abgrund auch in dich hinein.
trail: The German is aphorism 146 of Beyond Good and Evil (1886), in the chapter of ‘Maxims and Interludes.’ The abyss sentence is the second of two — it answers the warning about fighting monsters, and quoting it alone removes the thing it is about German and English ↗.

The public-domain English is Helen Zimmern’s 1906 translation: ‘He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee’ — archaic pronouns and ‘will also gaze’ Zimmern 1906, Project Gutenberg ↗.

The modern popular wording matches neither Zimmern nor Kaufmann (who has ‘look,’ not ‘gaze’). It is best described as Hollingdale’s 1973 verb choice with the pronouns modernised — which matters, because Hollingdale is still in copyright and Zimmern is not translations compared ↗.
source.excerptNote: Aphorism 146 entire, in Nietzsche’s German. The famous line is the second sentence; the first is the one that explains why he is talking about abysses at all.
source.rightsHolder: R. J. Hollingdale translation — for the popular English wording
source.rightsNote: Split. Nietzsche’s German is public domain worldwide (he died in 1900), so the original is free to quote, translate and reproduce. The English sentence in general circulation is a different matter: it tracks Hollingdale’s 1973 translation, which remains in copyright, as does Kaufmann’s 1966. If you want a free English text, use Helen Zimmern’s 1906 version — ‘And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee’ — or make your own translation from the German. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) published Beyond Good and Evil at his own expense in 1886; it sold poorly. Its fourth chapter is a sequence of free-standing epigrams, of which this is one. The abyss line has since escaped the book entirely — it turns up in films, songs and titles, usually detached from the monsters it was warning about, and usually in a translation nobody names.

copyAttribution: Wer mit Ungeheuern kämpft, mag zusehn, dass er nicht dabei zum Ungeheuer wird. Und wenn du lange in einen Abgrund blickst, blickt der Abgrund auch in dich hinein. —Friedrich Nietzsche, Jenseits von Gut und Böse §146 (1886). Public-domain English (Zimmern, 1906): "He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee."

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — check the translation and the missing half
misattribution.intro: Nobody doubts this is Nietzsche, and the citation is exact. The two things that go wrong are which English you are quoting, and the sentence that has been amputated from the front of it.

items.why: Aphorism 146 opens ‘He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster.’ The abyss is the second half of that warning — about what happens to people who spend their lives fighting something. Quoted alone it becomes a vague remark about staring into darkness full aphorism ↗.

The circulating English is not the public-domain Zimmern (‘if thou gaze… will also gaze into thee’) and not Kaufmann (‘look… looks’). It tracks Hollingdale’s 1973 wording with modernised pronouns, and it is quoted with no translator named compared ↗.
A pseudo-archaic version beginning ‘Battle not with monsters, lest ye become a monster’ circulates widely. It corresponds to no published translation and should not be presented as one.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil (1886), aphorism 146 — the German is free to reuse, but the English wording most people quote is a translation still in copyright public-domain alternative ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Read whole, it is a warning to people who have made an enemy their life’s work: the fight shapes the fighter, and prolonged attention to something changes the person paying attention. It is about moral contamination, not mystique.
Detached from the monsters, it has drifted into something closer to a horror-film epigraph — which is how most people now meet it, and why the abyss reads as a place rather than a habit.
detailsBody: German (1886): ‘Und wenn du lange in einen Abgrund blickst, blickt der Abgrund auch in dich hinein.’
Zimmern (1906, public domain): ‘And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee.’
Kaufmann (1966): ‘And when you look long into an abyss, the abyss also looks into you.’
Hollingdale (1973): ‘And when you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes also into you.’
Popular form: Hollingdale’s verbs, modernised pronouns, no translator credited.
